title: Learning to Explore: Scaling Agentic Reasoning via Exploration-Aware Policy Optimization
one_liner: Teach an interactive reasoning system to explore only when uncertainty is high, so it gathers missing facts without wasting steps once the task is already clear.
lead: Interactive reasoning systems can act before answering: they can inspect the environment, open menus, read pages, and test hypotheses. That freedom helps on hard tasks because some tasks cannot be solved until the system gathers extra facts, but it can also waste time because some tasks are already clear after one or two observations. A baseline that explores on every task spends many actions looking for information that it already has. This paper trains the policy to separate exploratory actions from execution actions. It rewards exploration when the action is likely to reduce uncertainty and stops rewarding it once the task state is clear. The result is a system that searches when information is missing and switches to execution as soon as the useful facts have been collected.

paras: On many tasks, an interactive system must decide whether to search for more information or act now. A naive strategy uses the same amount of exploration everywhere. That is inefficient because some tasks are already clear after one observation, while others remain ambiguous until the system inspects several sources.

Uniform exploration also harms training. If the reward does not distinguish useful information gathering from needless wandering, the learned policy cannot tell when one more action is worth paying for. The system either becomes timid and under-explores or becomes restless and keeps searching after the answer is already available.

callout.html: Reward exploration only when it is expected to reduce uncertainty, because good exploration closes an information gap and bad exploration just burns steps.

steps.text: Let the policy gather observations and act in the environment so training can see both good and bad search behavior.
Group actions that gather information apart from actions that directly complete the task because their value should be measured differently.
Give a reward to an exploratory action when it is expected to improve later decisions by reducing uncertainty.

steps.b: Optimize the policy with grouped rewards.
steps.text: Update the policy using separate signals for search and execution so each behavior is reinforced for the right reason.
Once the task state is understood, stop exploring and carry out the needed actions so the system does not waste steps.

paras: The paper changes the reinforcement-learning objective from one undifferentiated action reward into a reward that treats information gathering and task completion as different types of behavior.
object.object: the training reward over interactive action sequences

hidden.name: decision uncertainty at the current state
paras: The key hidden quantity is whether the system truly lacks enough information to choose the next action well. You cannot inspect that quantity directly. You only observe symptoms such as hesitation, contradictory evidence, or a wide spread over plausible next actions.

The paper tries to estimate this hidden uncertainty and use it to score exploration. An exploratory action is valuable when it narrows the set of plausible next moves, because that makes future execution more accurate and more direct.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark states or actions where search is genuinely helpful because it reduces uncertainty.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether one more search action will actually teach the system something useful for the next choice.
The method uses a fine-grained reward to value exploratory actions by their expected contribution to future decision quality, then optimizes them separately from execution actions.

paras: Search is beneficial only when it changes what the system should do next. If a page click, an inspection, or an environmental probe reveals a missing fact, then the exploratory step earns its keep because the next decision can be better informed. If the same action adds nothing, it is just delay.

By separating exploratory actions from execution actions during optimization, the method avoids mixing two incompatible goals into one signal. Exploration should be rewarded for reducing uncertainty, while execution should be rewarded for completing the task efficiently. That separation produces cleaner learning pressure because each behavior is judged on the role it is supposed to play.

The variational reward matters because it approximates future usefulness instead of scoring exploration only by immediate outcomes. An exploratory step can be good even before the final answer is known, provided it makes later decisions easier or safer.

math.words: A simple summary is to give exploratory actions credit when they reduce uncertainty about the next decision, while still adding the normal task-completion reward.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Run A explores twice, but only the first search reveals a missing setting.
Suppose task reward is 8, and the two search gains are 3 and 0.
Run B explores once, reveals nothing, and gets the same task reward 8.
Run B scores 8 + 0 = 8, so training prefers the search behavior that actually reduced uncertainty.

math.note: The full paper uses a more detailed reinforcement-learning objective, but this equation captures its main idea: exploration is good when it teaches the policy something useful for later action.

charts.title: Undifferentiated exploration
rows: steps spent after state is clear
charts.note: A baseline that searches without judging information value wastes many actions because it keeps exploring after the task is already understandable.

charts.title: Exploration-aware policy optimization
rows: steps spent after state is clear
charts.note: The paper reports consistent benchmark gains because the learned policy gathers missing facts early and then stops searching once the useful context is in hand.

items.html: If the training signal misjudges whether the state is ambiguous, then the policy may stop too early or keep exploring too long because the search reward is pointed at the wrong states.

items.b: Exploration labels can be too coarse.
items.html: Some actions both gather information and move the task forward, so a rigid grouping rule can mis-score them because it forces one action into only one category.

items.b: Search reward can overshadow task completion.
items.html: If lambda is too large, the policy may learn to chase information gain even when the task is already solvable because the training objective overpays for more searching.
The framework works when uncertainty estimates are calibrated and the search reward is balanced, because then the policy explores where the information gap is real and acts quickly elsewhere.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small web or text environment where some tasks are obvious after one observation and others require a few searches. Train one policy with a standard task reward and another with the exploration-aware grouped reward. Instrument the environment so you can count when search actions reveal previously missing facts and when later search actions reveal nothing new.

The demo should show that the exploration-aware policy takes more useful searches early on ambiguous tasks and fewer wasted searches on clear tasks, because the reward explicitly values uncertainty reduction instead of raw motion.
demo.closing: A convincing demo must show that selective exploration improves both task success and step efficiency, because the policy learns to search for information rather than search by habit.
